source: Nothing more happened on the passage worthy the mentioning; so, after a fine run, we safely arrived in Nantucket.

Nantucket! Take out your map and look at it. See what a real corner of the world it occupies; how it stands there, away off shore, more lonely than the Eddystone lighthouse. Look at it—a mere hillock, and elbow of sand; all beach, without a background. There is more sand there than you would use in twenty years as a substitute for blotting paper. Some gamesome wights will tell you that they have to plant weeds there, they don’t grow naturally; that they import Canada thistles; that they have to send beyond seas for a spile to stop a leak in an oil cask; that pieces of wood in Nantucket are carried about like bits of the true cross in Rome; that people there plant toadstools before their houses, to get under the shade in summer time; that one blade of grass makes an oasis, three blades in a day’s walk a prairie; that they wear quicksand shoes, something like Laplander snow-shoes; that they are so shut up, belted about, every way inclosed, surrounded, and made an utter island of by the ocean, that to their very chairs and tables small clams will sometimes be found adhering, as to the backs of sea turtles. But these extravaganzas only show that Nantucket is no Illinois.

Look now at the wondrous traditional story of how this island was settled by the red-men. Thus goes the legend. In olden times an eagle swooped down upon the New England coast, and carried off an infant Indian in his talons. With loud lament the parents saw their child borne out of sight over the wide waters. They resolved to follow in the same direction. Setting out in their canoes, after a perilous passage they discovered the island, and there they found an empty ivory casket,—the poor little Indian’s skeleton.

What wonder, then, that these Nantucketers, born on a beach, should take to the sea for a livelihood! They first caught crabs and quohogs in the sand; grown bolder, they waded out with nets for mackerel; more experienced, they pushed off in boats and captured cod; and at last, launching a navy of great ships on the sea, explored this watery world; put an incessant belt of circumnavigations round it; peeped in at Behring’s Straits; and in all seasons and all oceans declared everlasting war with the mightiest animated mass that has survived the flood; most monstrous and most mountainous! That Himmalehan, salt-sea Mastodon, clothed with such portentousness of unconscious power, that his very panics are more to be dreaded than his most fearless and malicious assaults!

And thus have these naked Nantucketers, these sea hermits, issuing from their ant-hill in the sea, overrun and conquered the watery world like so many Alexanders; parcelling out among them the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans, as the three pirate powers did Poland. Let America add Mexico to Texas, and pile Cuba upon Canada; let the English overswarm all India, and hang out their blazing banner from the sun; two thirds of this terraqueous globe are the Nantucketer’s. For the sea is his; he owns it, as Emperors own empires; other seamen having but a right of way through it. Merchant ships are but extension bridges; armed ones but floating forts; even pirates and privateers, though following the sea as highwaymen the road, they but plunder other ships, other fragments of the land like themselves, without seeking to draw their living from the bottomless deep itself. The Nantucketer, he alone resides and riots on the sea; he alone, in Bible language, goes down to it in ships; to and fro ploughing it as his own special plantation. There is his home; there lies his business, which a Noah’s flood would not interrupt, though it overwhelmed all the millions in China. He lives on the sea, as prairie cocks in the prairie; he hides among the waves, he climbs them as chamois hunters climb the Alps. For years he knows not the land; so that when he comes to it at last, it smells like another world, more strangely than the moon would to an Earthsman. With the landless gull, that at sunset folds her wings and is rocked to sleep between billows; so at nightfall, the Nantucketer, out of sight of land, furls his sails, and lays him to his rest, while under his very pillow rush herds of walruses and whales.

modern_en.title: Chapter 14 — Nantucket
paragraphs: Nothing else noteworthy happened during the crossing, so after a fine run, we arrived safely in Nantucket.

Nantucket! Take out your map and look at it. See what a real corner of the world it occupies; how it stands there, far offshore, lonelier than the Eddystone lighthouse. Look at it — a mere hillock, an elbow of sand; all beach, with no background. There is more sand there than you would use in twenty years as a substitute for blotting paper. Some playful fellows will tell you that they have to plant weeds there, since they don't grow naturally; that they import Canada thistles; that they have to send overseas for a wooden plug to stop a leak in an oil cask; that pieces of wood in Nantucket are carried about like bits of the true cross in Rome; that people there plant toadstools in front of their houses, to get under the shade in summertime; that one blade of grass makes an oasis, and three blades in a day's walk a prairie; that they wear quicksand shoes, something like Laplander snowshoes; that they are so shut in, belted about, enclosed every way, surrounded, and made an utter island of by the ocean, that small clams will sometimes be found sticking to their very chairs and tables, as to the backs of sea turtles. But these extravaganzas only show that Nantucket is no Illinois.

Now consider the marvelous traditional story of how the red men came to settle this island. The legend goes like this. Long ago an eagle swooped down on the New England coast and carried off an Indian baby in his talons. Wailing loudly, the parents watched their child carried away out of sight over the wide waters. They decided to follow in the same direction. They set out in their canoes, and after a dangerous crossing they found the island, and there they found an empty ivory casket — the poor little Indian's skeleton.

What wonder, then, that these Nantucketers, born on a beach, should take to the sea for a living! First they caught crabs and quahogs in the sand; grown bolder, they waded out with nets for mackerel; more experienced, they pushed off in boats and caught cod; and at last, launching a navy of great ships on the sea, they explored this watery world, put an unceasing belt of circumnavigations around it, peeped in at the Bering Strait, and in all seasons and all oceans declared everlasting war on the mightiest animated mass that has survived the flood — most monstrous and most mountainous! That Himalayan, salt-sea Mastodon, clothed with such an ominous weight of unconscious power that his very panics are more to be dreaded than his most fearless and malicious attacks!

And so these naked Nantucketers, these hermits of the sea, swarming out of their anthill in the ocean, have overrun and conquered the watery world like so many Alexanders, carving up the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans among themselves the way the three pirate powers carved up Poland. Let America add Mexico to Texas and stack Cuba on top of Canada; let the English swarm over all of India and hang their blazing flag from the sun; two thirds of this globe of land and water belong to the Nantucketer. For the sea is his; he owns it as emperors own empires, while other seamen have only a right of way through it. Merchant ships are nothing but extension bridges; warships nothing but floating forts; even pirates and privateers, though they follow the sea the way highwaymen follow the road, only rob other ships — other fragments of the land like themselves — without trying to make their living from the bottomless deep itself. The Nantucketer alone lives and revels on the sea; he alone, in the Bible's words, goes down to it in ships, plowing it back and forth as his own private plantation. That is his home; that is where his business lies, a business that Noah's flood would not interrupt, even if it drowned all the millions in China. He lives on the sea as prairie chickens live on the prairie; he hides among the waves, and he climbs them the way chamois hunters climb the Alps. For years at a time he doesn't know the land, so that when he finally reaches it, it smells like another world, stranger than the moon would smell to an earthling. Like the landless gull, which folds her wings at sunset and is rocked to sleep between the swells, the Nantucketer at nightfall, out of sight of land, furls his sails and lies down to rest, while under his very pillow herds of walruses and whales rush past.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 14 — Nantucket
paragraphs: Der skete ikke andet bemærkelsesværdigt under overfarten, så efter en fin sejlads nåede vi sikkert frem til Nantucket.

Nantucket! Tag dit kort frem og se på det. Se, hvilket virkeligt hjørne af verden den ligger i; hvordan den ligger der, langt ude til havs, ensommere end Eddystone-fyrtårnet. Se på den — en ren høj, en albue af sand, alt strand og ingen baggrund. Der er mere sand der, end du ville bruge på tyve år som erstatning for trækpapir. Nogle spøgefugle vil fortælle dig, at de er nødt til at plante ukrudt der, fordi det ikke vokser af sig selv; at de importerer canadiske tidsler; at de må sende over havet efter en træprop til at stoppe en utæthed i en tranfustage; at stykker af træ i Nantucket bæres rundt som stumper af det sande kors i Rom; at folk planter fluesvampe foran deres huse for at få skygge om sommeren; at ét græsstrå gør en oase, og tre strå på en dagsmarch en prærie; at de går på kviksandssko, noget i retning af lappernes snesko; at de er så lukket inde, spændt ind, omringet på alle sider og gjort til en helt og aldeles ø af havet, at små muslinger undertiden sidder fast på selve deres stole og borde, som på ryggen af havskildpadder. Men disse overdrivelser viser kun, at Nantucket ikke er Illinois.

Tænk nu på den vidunderlige overleverede historie om, hvordan de rødhudede kom til at slå sig ned på denne ø. Legenden lyder sådan. For længe siden slog en ørn ned over kysten af New England og bar et indianerbarn af sted i sine kløer. Forældrene så højlydt jamrende deres barn blive båret ud af syne over de vide vande. De besluttede at følge efter i samme retning. De tog af sted i deres kanoer, og efter en farlig overfart fandt de øen, og dér fandt de et tomt elfenbensskrin — den stakkels lille indianers skelet.

Er det så underligt, at disse nantucketfolk, født på en strand, tager til søs for at tjene til livet! Først fangede de krabber og kvahogmuslinger i sandet. Som de blev dristigere, vadede de ud med garn efter makrel. Som de blev mere erfarne, skubbede de fra land i både og fangede torsk. Og til sidst sendte de en hel flåde af store skibe ud på havet, udforskede denne vandverden, lagde et uophørligt bælte af jordomsejlinger rundt om den, kiggede ind i Beringstrædet og erklærede til alle årstider og i alle have evig krig mod den mægtigste levende masse, der har overlevet syndfloden — mest uhyrlig og mest bjergagtig! Den himalayaagtige, saltvandsmastodont, klædt i en så uhyggelig vægt af ubevidst kraft, at hans panik er mere at frygte end hans mest frygtløse og ondsindede angreb!

Og sådan har disse nøgne nantucketere, disse havets eneboere, vrimlende ud af deres myretue i havet, oversvømmet og erobret vandverdenen som så mange Alexandre og delt Atlanterhavet, Stillehavet og Det Indiske Ocean imellem sig, ligesom de tre røvermagter delte Polen. Lad Amerika lægge Mexico til Texas og stable Cuba oven på Canada. Lad englænderne vrimle ud over hele Indien og hænge deres flammende flag op fra solen. To tredjedele af denne klode af land og vand tilhører nantucketeren. For havet er hans. Han ejer det, som kejsere ejer riger, mens andre søfolk kun har ret til at færdes igennem det. Handelsskibe er intet andet end forlængede broer, krigsskibe intet andet end flydende fæstninger. Selv sørøvere og kaprere, skønt de følger havet, som landevejsrøvere følger vejen, plyndrer kun andre skibe — andre stumper af landet ligesom dem selv — uden at prøve at leve af selve det bundløse dyb. Kun nantucketeren lever og fryder sig på havet. Kun han farer, med Bibelens ord, ned på det i skibe og pløjer det frem og tilbage som sin egen private plantage. Det er hans hjem. Det er der, hans forretning ligger, en forretning som Noas syndflod ikke ville afbryde, selv om den druknede alle millioner i Kina. Han lever på havet, som præriehøns lever på prærien. Han skjuler sig blandt bølgerne, og han klatrer op ad dem, som gemsejægere klatrer i Alperne. I årevis ad gangen kender han ikke landet, så når han endelig når det, dufter det som en anden verden, mere fremmed, end månen ville dufte for et jordmenneske. Som den landløse måge, der folder sine vinger ved solnedgang og vugges i søvn mellem dønningerne, tager nantucketeren om aftenen, ude af syne af land, sine sejl ind og lægger sig til hvile, mens flokke af hvalrosser og hvaler stormer forbi lige under hans pude.
